title: A spread of western North Pacific delays reduced CalCOFI oxygen error in a 2007-2020 retrospective test
abstract: We tested whether a spread of transport delays can reduce the western oxygen recovery before it reaches California on sigma0 26.5. We used two published annual within-type oxygen indices and nonnegative kernels with delays of 5-25 years and gain at most one. A fit through 2006 gave a 2007-2020 RMS error of 6.25 umol/kg, against 12.87 for one delay, 10.65 for persistence and 7.55 for a trend. It still predicted too little loss: the evaluation mean was -10.36 against -14.15 observed. Global optimization showed that the frozen 1984-2020 records need a delay interval at least 8 years wide to keep every annual error below 4 umol/kg. This is conditional on exact inputs. A single delay can fit within 5 umol/kg if source years can change by up to 2.13 annual bootstrap SDs. Small increases in allowed training error also give broad prediction ranges. Dispersed transport can improve the prediction but does not identify parcel ages or fully explain the California loss. Only one retrospective split is tested, and the parent indices use full-record processing.
